title: A lattice oxygen-free design for efficient and stable photothermal methane dry reforming

paper_content.abstract: Photothermal dry reforming of methane, a promising approach to producing syngas, typically uses oxide materials and is mediated by lattice oxygen. However, it is limited by the balance of the oxygen-releasing/replenishing loop. Here, we present a methane activation pathway free of lattice oxygen on a N-Ni/NiCo@C catalyst. Direct involvement of reactive oxygen species (O*/OH*) released from CO2 promotes effective CH4 activation and eliminates coke deposition on oxophilic NiCo sites. Control experiments and density functional theory calculations show that forming a C-N-Ni structure is essential for improving catalytic performance. This is achieved by strengthening the electronic interaction between the NiCo nanoparticles and the carbon layer, thereby boosting the elemental steps of CH4 dehydrogenation and CHx oxidation and preventing metal oxidation. The optimal catalyst exhibits a high light-to-chemical energy efficiency of 52%, maintaining stability during 200 hours of continuous operation at a mild temperature of 540 °C. This work demonstrates that highly efficient and stable photothermal dry reforming of methane can be achieved by bypassing lattice oxygen.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this study, the authors report a N-Ni/NiCo@C catalyst for highly efficient and stable photo-thermal methane dry reforming, which is distinct from the conventional metal oxide-supported catalysts. The structure-activity relationship investigation reveals the synergistic effect among the precise catalyst structure, involved carbon layer encapsulation, C-N-Ni electron transfer channels, and highly dispersed nano Ni/Co alloy particles, achieving high light utilization efficiency, performance, and stability. Furthermore, in situ characterization reveals a CH4 activation pathway that is free of lattice oxygen. The substantial O* released from CO2 is adsorbed on oxophilic NiCo alloy, and then effectively oxidizes the carbon species (CH*) into CHO*, with the assistance of photo-generated holes. The findings in this work are interesting, offering a novel strategy for producing long-term stable NiCo-based catalysts for photo-thermal methane dry reforming. Minor revision is recommended, and the following comments and suggestions should be addressed.
1. H2 atmosphere is a typical atmosphere for preparing metallic state catalysts. Why does this paper use the inert gas Ar? Does the gas composition affect the metal dispersion?
2. Given that the performance evaluation conditions for the photo-thermal DRM reaction vary in different literature and the data on light utilization efficiency is often missing, how can the comparability of the data in this work (LTCEE) and those in the literature be ensured?
3. Using XRD, Raman, and XPS to observe the carbon deposits may not be precise enough. Employing TGA or TG-MS for carbon deposit quantification is strongly recommended.
4. Ni/Co catalysts supported on common metal oxides tend to agglomerate easily during DRM reactions. Imaging technology is recommended to calculate the particle size of spent catalysts for further verification of sintering resistance.
5. How was the existence of C-N-Ni sites determined? Is it possible that the NiN phase was formed and contributed to the DRM reaction?
6. The catalytic performance was measured at 600 °C in this manuscript, and it was proved that the carbon in the material would not be oxidized to CO. However, traditional dry reforming of methane requires a temperature of 700-800 °C. What is the maximum temperature at which this type of C-coated catalyst can be used?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This study reports a metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived N-doped NiCo nanoalloy catalyst (N-Ni/NiCo@C) for photothermal methane dry reforming. The core innovation resides in circumventing the traditional lattice oxygen-dependent reaction pathway in catalysis; instead, efficient methane activation and exceptional anti-coking stability are achieved through the deliberate construction of a C-N-Ni coordination structure. The authors have conducted systematic and in-depth investigations encompassing experimental design, advanced characterization techniques, and theoretical calculations, with conclusions well-supported by sufficient data and rigorous reasoning. As a result, I recommend the acceptance of this manuscript for publication after addressing the following issues.
1.How did the authors ensure the successful preparation of the NiCo bimetallic MOF? Characterization of the MOF precursor should also be provided.
2.The authors mention in the Supplementary Information that the reactant conversion rates and product production rates are calculated based on the outlet flow stream. It is requested to clarify how the outlet flow rate is obtained: whether it is directly measured using mass flow meters or derived from N2 balance calculations.
3.For Fig. 2b, the authors mention that it presents comparative results of photothermal and pure thermal conversion rates measured at the same temperature. It is noteworthy that the authors need to specify whether this temperature refers to the bulk temperature of the catalyst powder (measured by a thermocouple) or the set temperature of the electric heating component in the reactor. This clarification directly impacts the validity of the definition for light-to-chemical energy efficiency.
4.In the mechanism study, the authors state that light irradiation generates carboxyl intermediates (-COOH) at 1538 cm-1. However, according to the in situ DRIFTS spectra under both dark and light conditions, the peak at 1538 cm-1 can be observed in both cases. If the authors consider the positive and negative peaks at 1538 cm-1 as corresponding to different species, how to interpret the negative peak in PDRM at 300℃? It is recommended that the authors re-analyze the in situ DRIFTS spectra.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, a photothermal DRM reaction on a nitrogen-doped carbon-coated N-Ni/NiCo@C catalyst was reported. Different from the traditional oxygen involved semiconductor-based catalyst, this material structure for solar DRM would be new and the performance is good. Mechanism investigation and explanation would also interest a wide readship compared to the conventional ‘lattice oxygen’ involving Mars-van Krevelen pathway. In addition, the experiments were systematically and well conducted in most parts. A Minor Revision would be recommended and following comments and suggestions should be properly addressed and corrected.
(1) The manuscript attributes the remarkable 200-h stability primarily to the electronic effect of the C–N–Ni site, which is proposed to suppress oxidation. This interpretation overlooks a more obvious factor: the physical confinement and encapsulation provided by the graphitic carbon layer. Although the authors report a drastic stability difference between N-Ni/NiCo@C and the NiCo/Al2O3 reference, these systems differ in at least two major respects: (i) the presence of the proposed C–N–Ni site and (ii) the carbon surface itself. Hence, the enhanced durability cannot be unambiguously assigned to the C–N–Ni site without decoupling these effects.
(2) ICP–OES indicates severe Ni loss upon increasing N-doping (28.3 to 3.1 wt%). The authors should clarify the origin of this depletion and reconcile it with the proposed stabilization mechanism.
(3) The mapping shows clear O signals (Figure 1e), which conflicts with the “lattice-oxygen-free” claim as presently phrased. Please (i) define the scope of “lattice-oxygen-free” (bulk vs. surface) and (ii) pinpoint the oxygen’s location—carbon-support functionalities vs. an alloy oxide overlayer—to avoid a potentially misleading title.
(4) The authors state that “the Ni 2p spectra show the Ni2+ peak (856.2 eV) shifts by +0.77 eV from N0 to N1.” However, the plotted positions indicate a −0.77 eV shift (i.e., to lower binding energy) from N0 to N1. Please double check the sign and report the absolute peak positions for both samples.

### Reviewer 1

In this study, the authors report a N-Ni/NiCo@C catalyst for highly efficient and stable photo-thermal methane dry reforming, which is distinct from the conventional metal oxide-supported catalysts. The structure-activity relationship investigation reveals the synergistic effect among the precise catalyst structure, involved carbon layer encapsulation, C-N-Ni electron transfer channels, and highly dispersed nano Ni/Co alloy particles, achieving high light utilization efficiency, performance, and stability. Furthermore, in situ characterization reveals a CH4 activation pathway that is free of lattice oxygen. The substantial O* released from CO2 is adsorbed on oxophilic NiCo alloy, and then effectively oxidizes the carbon species (CH*) into CHO*, with the assistance of photo-generated holes. The findings in this work are interesting, offering a novel strategy for producing long-term stable NiCo-based catalysts for photo-thermal methane dry reforming. Minor revision is recommended, and the following comments and suggestions should be addressed.
1. H2 atmosphere is a typical atmosphere for preparing metallic state catalysts. Why does this paper use the inert gas Ar? Does the gas composition affect the metal dispersion?
2. Given that the performance evaluation conditions for the photo-thermal DRM reaction vary in different literature and the data on light utilization efficiency is often missing, how can the comparability of the data in this work (LTCEE) and those in the literature be ensured?
3. Using XRD, Raman, and XPS to observe the carbon deposits may not be precise enough. Employing TGA or TG-MS for carbon deposit quantification is strongly recommended.
4. Ni/Co catalysts supported on common metal oxides tend to agglomerate easily during DRM reactions. Imaging technology is recommended to calculate the particle size of spent catalysts for further verification of sintering resistance.
5. How was the existence of C-N-Ni sites determined? Is it possible that the NiN phase was formed and contributed to the DRM reaction?
6. The catalytic performance was measured at 600 °C in this manuscript, and it was proved that the carbon in the material would not be oxidized to CO. However, traditional dry reforming of methane requires a temperature of 700-800 °C. What is the maximum temperature at which this type of C-coated catalyst can be used?

### Reviewer 2

This study reports a metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived N-doped NiCo nanoalloy catalyst (N-Ni/NiCo@C) for photothermal methane dry reforming. The core innovation resides in circumventing the traditional lattice oxygen-dependent reaction pathway in catalysis; instead, efficient methane activation and exceptional anti-coking stability are achieved through the deliberate construction of a C-N-Ni coordination structure. The authors have conducted systematic and in-depth investigations encompassing experimental design, advanced characterization techniques, and theoretical calculations, with conclusions well-supported by sufficient data and rigorous reasoning. As a result, I recommend the acceptance of this manuscript for publication after addressing the following issues.
1.How did the authors ensure the successful preparation of the NiCo bimetallic MOF? Characterization of the MOF precursor should also be provided.
2.The authors mention in the Supplementary Information that the reactant conversion rates and product production rates are calculated based on the outlet flow stream. It is requested to clarify how the outlet flow rate is obtained: whether it is directly measured using mass flow meters or derived from N2 balance calculations.
3.For Fig. 2b, the authors mention that it presents comparative results of photothermal and pure thermal conversion rates measured at the same temperature. It is noteworthy that the authors need to specify whether this temperature refers to the bulk temperature of the catalyst powder (measured by a thermocouple) or the set temperature of the electric heating component in the reactor. This clarification directly impacts the validity of the definition for light-to-chemical energy efficiency.
4.In the mechanism study, the authors state that light irradiation generates carboxyl intermediates (-COOH) at 1538 cm-1. However, according to the in situ DRIFTS spectra under both dark and light conditions, the peak at 1538 cm-1 can be observed in both cases. If the authors consider the positive and negative peaks at 1538 cm-1 as corresponding to different species, how to interpret the negative peak in PDRM at 300℃? It is recommended that the authors re-analyze the in situ DRIFTS spectra.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, a photothermal DRM reaction on a nitrogen-doped carbon-coated N-Ni/NiCo@C catalyst was reported. Different from the traditional oxygen involved semiconductor-based catalyst, this material structure for solar DRM would be new and the performance is good. Mechanism investigation and explanation would also interest a wide readship compared to the conventional ‘lattice oxygen’ involving Mars-van Krevelen pathway. In addition, the experiments were systematically and well conducted in most parts. A Minor Revision would be recommended and following comments and suggestions should be properly addressed and corrected.
(1) The manuscript attributes the remarkable 200-h stability primarily to the electronic effect of the C–N–Ni site, which is proposed to suppress oxidation. This interpretation overlooks a more obvious factor: the physical confinement and encapsulation provided by the graphitic carbon layer. Although the authors report a drastic stability difference between N-Ni/NiCo@C and the NiCo/Al2O3 reference, these systems differ in at least two major respects: (i) the presence of the proposed C–N–Ni site and (ii) the carbon surface itself. ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this study, the authors report a N-Ni/NiCo@C catalyst for highly efficient and stable photo-thermal methane dry reforming, which is distinct from the conventional metal oxide-supported catalysts. The structure-activity relationship investigation reveals the synergistic effect among the precise catalyst structure, involved carbon layer encapsulation, C-N-Ni electron transfer channels, and highly dispersed nano Ni/Co alloy particles, achieving high light utilization efficiency, performance, and stability. Furthermore, in situ characterization reveals a CH4 activation pathway that is free of lattice oxygen. The substantial O* released from CO2 is adsorbed on oxophilic NiCo alloy, and then effectively oxidizes the carbon species (CH*) into CHO*, with the assistance of photo-generated holes. The findings in this work are interesting, offering a novel strategy for producing long-term stable NiCo-based catalysts for photo-thermal methane dry reforming. Minor revision is recommended, and the following comments and suggestions should be addressed.
1. H2 atmosphere is a typical atmosphere for preparing metallic state catalysts. Why does this paper use the inert gas Ar? Does the gas composition affect the metal dispersion?
2. Given that the performance evaluation conditions for the photo-thermal DRM reaction vary in different literature and the data on light utilization efficiency is often missing, how can the comparability of the data in this work (LTCEE) and those in the literature be ensured?
3. Using XRD, Raman, and XPS to observe the carbon deposits may not be precise enough. Employing TGA or TG-MS for carbon deposit quantification is strongly recommended.
4. Ni/Co catalysts supported on common metal oxides tend to agglomerate easily during DRM reactions. Imaging technology is recommended to calculate the particle size of spent catalysts for further verification of sintering resistance.
5. How was the existence of C-N-Ni sites determined? Is it possible that the NiN phase was formed and contributed to the DRM reaction?
6. The catalytic performance was measured at 600 °C in this manuscript, and it was proved that the carbon in the material would not be oxidized to CO. However, traditional dry reforming of methane requires a temperature of 700-800 °C. What is the maximum temperature at which this type of C-coated catalyst can be used?

### Reviewer 2

This study reports a metal-organic framework (MOF)-derived N-doped NiCo nanoalloy catalyst (N-Ni/NiCo@C) for photothermal methane dry reforming. The core innovation resides in circumventing the traditional lattice oxygen-dependent reaction pathway in catalysis; instead, efficient methane activation and exceptional anti-coking stability are achieved through the deliberate construction of a C-N-Ni coordination structure. The authors have conducted systematic and in-depth investigations encompassing experimental design, advanced characterization techniques, and theoretical calculations, with conclusions well-supported by sufficient data and rigorous reasoning. As a result, I recommend the acceptance of this manuscript for publication after addressing the following issues.
1.How did the authors ensure the successful preparation of the NiCo bimetallic MOF? Characterization of the MOF precursor should also be provided.
2.The authors mention in the Supplementary Information that the reactant conversion rates and product production rates are calculated based on the outlet flow stream. It is requested to clarify how the outlet flow rate is obtained: whether it is directly measured using mass flow meters or derived from N2 balance calculations.
3.For Fig. 2b, the authors mention that it presents comparative results of photothermal and pure thermal conversion rates measured at the same temperature. It is noteworthy that the authors need to specify whether this temperature refers to the bulk temperature of the catalyst powder (measured by a thermocouple) or the set temperature of the electric heating component in the reactor. This clarification directly impacts the validity of the definition for light-to-chemical energy efficiency.
4.In the mechanism study, the authors state that light irradiation generates carboxyl intermediates (-COOH) at 1538 cm-1. However, according to the in situ DRIFTS spectra under both dark and light conditions, the peak at 1538 cm-1 can be observed in both cases. If the authors consider the positive and negative peaks at 1538 cm-1 as corresponding to different species, how to interpret the negative peak in PDRM at 300℃? It is recommended that the authors re-analyze the in situ DRIFTS spectra.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, a photothermal DRM reaction on a nitrogen-doped carbon-coated N-Ni/NiCo@C catalyst was reported. Different from the traditional oxygen involved semiconductor-based catalyst, this material structure for solar DRM would be new and the performance is good. Mechanism investigation and explanation would also interest a wide readship compared to the conventional ‘lattice oxygen’ involving Mars-van Krevelen pathway. In addition, the experiments were systematically and well conducted in most parts. A Minor Revision would be recommended and following comments and suggestions should be properly addressed and corrected.
(1) The manuscript attributes the remarkable 200-h stability primarily to the electronic effect of the C–N–Ni site, which is proposed to suppress oxidation. This interpretation overlooks a more obvious factor: the physical confinement and encapsulation provided by the graphitic carbon layer. Although the authors report a drastic stability difference between N-Ni/NiCo@C and the NiCo/Al2O3 reference, these systems differ in at least two major respects: (i) the presence of the proposed C–N–Ni site and (ii) the carbon surface itself. Hence, the enhanced durability cannot be unambiguously assigned to the C–N–Ni site without decoupling these effects.
(2) ICP–OES indicates severe Ni loss upon increasing N-doping (28.3 to 3.1 wt%). The authors should clarify the origin of this depletion and reconcile it with the proposed stabilization mechanism.
(3) The mapping shows clear O signals (Figure 1e), which conflicts with the “lattice-oxygen-free” claim as presently phrased. Please (i) define the scope of “lattice-oxygen-free” (bulk vs. surface) and (ii) pinpoint the oxygen’s location—carbon-support functionalities vs. an alloy oxide overlayer—to avoid a potentially misleading title.
(4) The authors state that “the Ni 2p spectra show the Ni2+ peak (856.2 eV) shifts by +0.77 eV from N0 to N1.” However, the plotted positions indicate a −0.77 eV shift (i.e., to lower binding energy) from N0 to N1. Please double check the sign and report the absolute peak positions for both samples.
